sentences.text: Amphicoelias was a moderately sized sauropod, reaching about 18 meters in length and weighing 15 metric tons, which is shorter than its relative Diplodocus.
This animal had very long and thin hindlimbs and forelimbs that were proportionally longer than in its relatives.
Amphicoelias possessed amphicoelous vertebrae, meaning both ends of the centrum were mildly to moderately concave.
The species Amphicoelias altus was approximately 25 meters long, similar in size to Diplodocus.
Early estimates suggested Amphicoelias fragillimus could have been between 40 and 60 meters long, based on a 2.7-meter dorsal vertebra.
Some researchers argue that a typographical error in the original scale bar means the vertebra of A. fragillimus was actually only 1.38 meters tall.
The genus Amphicoelias was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1878.
Fossils were discovered in 1877 by Oramel William Lucas in rock outcrops near Cañon City, Colorado.
The holotype specimen of Amphicoelias altus, cataloged as AMNH 5764, contains uncertain material regarding which bones belong to the species.
The femur of Amphicoelias latus measures 1.4 meters in length, though its proximal end is incomplete.
Amphicoelias lived in a savanna-like environment where poor-quality food likely drove the evolution of its giant size.
Studies of giant mammalian herbivores like elephants and rhinos suggest that larger size improves food digestion efficiency in plant-eating animals.
Sauropod dinosaurs throughout their history lived primarily in semi-arid, seasonally dry environments with seasonal drops in food quality.
Carpenter argued that the sauropod digestive system's adaptation to low-quality food allowed ferns to be a major part of their diet.
Large animals have longer digestive systems that retain food for longer periods, allowing them to survive on low-quality food sources.
Amphicoelias lived in an essentially savanna environment, supporting the idea that poor-quality food in arid settings promotes the evolution of giant herbivores.
Researchers suggest that benefits like predator immunity and longer lifespans were secondary advantages of the giant size of Amphicoelias.
Carpenter speculated that Amphicoelias may have used gallery forests for shade during the day and fed on the savanna at night.
Carpenter suggested that predator immunity, lower energy costs, and longer life are likely secondary advantages of large size.
Cope placed it in a unique family, Amphicoeliidae, which is now considered a nomen oblitum (forgotten name).
Amphicoelias belongs to the parent group Diplodocoidea.
In 2007, John Foster suggested that differences between A. altus and Diplodocus are not significant and may result from individual variation.
Emanuel Tschopp and colleagues disputed the synonymy of Amphicoelias and Diplodocus in a 2015 phylogenetic analysis.
While most scientists distinguish Amphicoelias and Diplodocus as separate genera, at least one researcher suggests Amphicoelias is likely the older synonym of Diplodocus.
A cladogram shows the relationships of A. altus with other diplodocids based on the analysis by Tschopp and Mateus in 2017.
Amphicoelias altus lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 150 to 145 million years ago (Kimmeridgian and Tithonian stages), in what is now North America.
Collection data determined the specimen came from the youngest layers of the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation, separate from the layers containing Camarasaurus fossils.

The presence of dinosaurs like Camarasaurus in the same rocks suggests the site belongs to the Morrison Formation, dating it to 150 million years ago in the late Jurassic period, specifically the Tithonian.

In 1881, Othniel Charles Marsh found Amphicoeliidae and Amphicoelias to be intermediate and poorly defined, noting that the primary feature of mildly concave articular faces was widespread in sauropods like Brontosaurus excelsus.
